The first mini project was about simulation and used many techniques that we saw later on in the course. It was the first time we looped through a function which we did many times later with both bootstrapping and empirical power tests. We also used many density functions that we worked with a lot throughout the semester such as the exponential and beta distribution. My biggest takeaway form mini project 1 was probably how useful simulation can be in statistics and I thoguth it was cool that the theoretcial results were closely matched with the simulated results, 


The second mini project was about showing our understanding of different statistical terms and to use them in context of a meaningful story. This is something that has been important throughout the course as we have been prompted to interpret results in context of a problem and explain certain statistical terms or techniques in plain English throughout the course. This project really made me think about the meaning of the terms we had been using so far in the semester and it challenged my understanding of the concepts in a good way. 

This project was somewhat similar to mini project 5 where we answered questions based of an article arguing that relying on arbitrary thresholds for p-value is not statistically sounds. Both these projects were geared towards a higher level understanding of concepts than actual calculations. I had many takeaways from this article and the put a lot of thoguht into my answers. Something that will stick with me is when the authors said that there is no statistically significant difference between a significant and insignificant test. I think this shows why relying solely on a p-value in research is not a good idea. 

Mini project 3 was about confidence interval assumptions and brought back some simulation techniques such as looping through a function from mini project 1. This project showcased the importance of assumptions and the consequences if assumptions are broken, something that we have talked about throughout the course and something I remember talking about in stat 113. My biggest takewaya is definitely how important it is to be aware of all assumptions you are making about your data and model and to try and address them in the best way possible. The project showcased the importance of assumptions and the consequences to our results when the assumptions are broken. 

This ties into mini project 4 about Bayesian analysis well because we had to understand the assumptions of our prior distributions. In mini project 4 we worked with different prior distributions to reach a posterior distribution and it was important to know what assumptions each prior distribution assumed to be true. Apart from the assumption and interpreting in context part of mini project 4, it kind of stood out among the projects as it was the only project where we did not have a frequentist approach. My biggest takeaway from this project is the importance of understanding your prior distribution because of the impact it can have on your results. I think Bayesian analysis was very interesting and the project showed us how useful it can be.
